reference_title: Ground Modification Methods Reference Manual – Volume I

sections.title: Description and History
sections.summary: Opening part of Chapter 4 (pp. 4-1 to 4-13): describes deep compaction, its history, the chapter's scope, alternative technologies and solutions, liquefaction mitigation assessment, a glossary and the primary references for deep dynamic compaction (DDC) and vibro-compaction (VC).
sections.body: Part 1.0 of the chapter (pp. 4-1 to 4-13) introduces deep compaction. It describes the two methods treated in detail, deep dynamic compaction and vibro-compaction, gives their historical development, states the focus and scope of the chapter, lists alternative densification technologies and alternative foundation solutions, outlines how liquefaction potential and its mitigation are assessed, and closes with a glossary and the primary references for each method.
sections.applicability: Orientation to deep dynamic compaction and vibro-compaction before feasibility and design.

sections.title: Description
sections.summary: Deep compaction uses dynamic methods to impart high energy to loose cohesionless soils with little or no fines. DDC drops a 10 to 40 kip tamper 30 to 100 ft, improving 10 to 35 ft; vibro-compaction uses depth vibrators with horizontal vibration. Results: higher bearing and shear strength, less settlement, more liquefaction resistance.
sections.body: Deep compaction is a category of technologies that impart high levels of energy to the ground dynamically to improve soil properties. They are most applicable to loose cohesionless soils with little to no fines, and the densification increases bearing capacity and shear strength, reduces settlement and increases liquefaction resistance (p. 4-1). Two methods are treated in detail: Deep Dynamic Compaction (DDC), which densifies by drop weights impacting the surface, and Vibro-compaction (VC), which lowers vibrators into the loose soil to send out horizontal vibrations. Related methods are blast densification, rapid impact compaction and vibro-replacement (Chapter 5). In DDC a tamper of 10 to 40 kips is repeatedly raised and dropped from 30 to 100 ft by a conventional crane with a single cable and a free-spool winch; depth of improvement is proportional to energy and generally ranges from 10 to 35 ft for light to heavy energy. The surface left loose to crater depth is then compacted on a tight grid with a low-energy ironing pass (Figure 4-1). DDC is generally the most economical form of site improvement, usable in deposits from silty soils to boulder-sized granular fill, natural or fill (p. 4-2). Vibro-compaction, originally called vibroflotation because it used water jetting, uses probe-type depth vibrators in loose sands and gravels (Figure 4-2); most projects use the wet (jetting) method. Vibration and water nullify the effective stresses between grains, which rearrange under gravity to the densest possible state; next to the vibrator the saturated soil liquefies locally and temporarily (Moseley and Priebe 1993). VC results: increased bearing resistance permitting shallow foundations, reduced settlement, increased liquefaction resistance and shear strength, reduced permeability, and filling of voids (p. 4-3). Results depend on soil type and gradation, point spacing, equipment and compaction duration.
key_points: DDC tamper 10 to 40 kips dropped 30 to 100 ft; depth of improvement generally 10 to 35 ft (p. 4-1).
An ironing pass (low-level energy on a tight grid) compacts the surface left loose to crater depth.
Deep compaction is most applicable to loose cohesionless soils with little to no fines.
Most vibro-compaction is done by the wet (water jetting) method (p. 4-3).
VC outcome depends on in situ soil type and gradation, point spacing, equipment, and compaction duration.

sections.title: Historical Overview
sections.summary: Container heading for the historical development of the two methods: deep dynamic compaction (impact tamping to the 1975 depth formula) and vibro-compaction (vibroflotation from the 1930s to seismic mitigation) (pp. 4-4 to 4-5).
sections.body: This heading introduces two subsections tracing the historical development of deep dynamic compaction (impact tamping from early practice to the 1975 depth-of-improvement formula and FHWA guidance) and of vibro-compaction (vibroflotation from the early 1930s to modern use for liquefaction mitigation).
sections.applicability: Background on how DDC and VC practice developed.

sections.title: Deep Dynamic Compaction
sections.summary: History of DDC: early tamping, regular use from 1969 (European practice) and 1971 (U.S.), the names heavy tamping, dynamic consolidation and dynamic compaction, and the 1975 Menard and Broise formula relating depth of improvement to applied energy; FHWA 1986 and GEC 1 1995 guidelines.
sections.body: Impacting soils with dropped tampers is centuries old (Kerisel 1985). Cohesionless soils were compacted with a 4 kip tamper and 5 ft drop in 1933 (Loos 1963); the Corps of Engineers experimented with heavy tamping in 1936 (USACE 1938); dynamic compaction densified loose soils for a 250 ft diameter crude oil tank in 1955 (Hobbs 1976); heavy tampers compacted loessial silty and sandy soils from about 1960 (Bobylev 1963) (p. 4-4). Regular use began in European practice in 1969 and U.S. practice in 1971. European practice dropped 18 to 22 kip tampers 25 to 40 ft on good fill (rock waste, rubble, sand), called heavy tamping, later extended to fine-grained deposits as dynamic consolidation (Menard and Broise 1975). U.S. practice initially used 4 to 12 kip tampers with 20 to 35 ft drops on loose rubble fill and granular deposits for lightly loaded structures, later up to 33 kips on former landfills; first called pounding, then dynamic compaction (FHWA 1986). The manual uses deep dynamic compaction to distinguish it from shallow methods such as high energy impact rollers. Menard and Broise (1975) presented a formula predicting depth of improvement from applied energy, placing the process on a sound technical basis. U.S. practice was summarized in FHWA (1986), and guidelines have been kept current in FHWA (1986), GEC 1 (1995) and this manual.
key_points: Regular use began in 1969 (European practice) and 1971 (U.S. practice) (p. 4-4).
Menard and Broise (1975) gave the first formula for depth of improvement versus applied energy.
The term deep dynamic compaction distinguishes it from shallow dynamic methods such as high energy impact rollers.
Current U.S. guidance: FHWA (1986), GEC 1 (1995) and this manual.
sections.applicability: Historical context and source lineage for DDC design guidance.

sections.title: Vibro-compaction
sections.summary: History of vibro-compaction: developed in the early 1930s to compact loose sands to 65 ft with a vibrating probe and water jetting (vibroflotation); first U.S. project 1948; accepted by the early 1970s as the premier method for deep sand; vibroflot (horizontal) versus top-pile vibrator systems (vertical); improved ground performing well in earthquakes.
sections.body: The concept was developed in the early 1930s for compacting variable, loose natural sand deposits to depths of 65 ft, including underwater sands for seaport developments, replacing surface vibration or rolling. A metal tube or probe with an electric motor driving an eccentric weight in its lower end was inserted into the ground, with pressurized water jetted through the tip to assist penetration; the process was patented as Vibroflotation (p. 4-5). The first U.S. project was in 1948, and by the early 1970s vibro-compaction was generally accepted as the premier method of densifying deep sand deposits. Systems historically identified as vibro-compaction include vibroflotation and the vibratory beam. Vibroflotation uses a vibroprobe (vibroflot) that densifies with predominantly horizontal vibrations; other techniques use a top pile vibrator that densifies with predominantly vertical vibrations, normally requiring closer spacing and being less efficient (Welsh 1986; Schaefer 1997). Major earthquakes of 1964 brought liquefaction to the forefront, and later earthquakes highlighted the importance of ground improvement on seismically unstable sites: observations showed that sites treated by vibro-densification either precluded liquefaction or limited deformations to a minimum while untreated areas showed settlements and sand boils.
key_points: Developed in the early 1930s for loose sands to depths of 65 ft (p. 4-5).
First U.S. project 1948; premier deep-sand densification method by the early 1970s.
Vibroflot = predominantly horizontal vibrations; top pile vibrator systems = predominantly vertical vibrations, closer spacing, less efficient.
Vibro-densified sites have precluded liquefaction or limited deformations in earthquakes.
sections.applicability: Historical context for vibro-compaction and its seismic performance record.

sections.title: Focus and Scope
sections.summary: DDC and vibro-compaction are mature, well-established ground modification methods; the chapter gives an overview and the state of practice covering feasibility, equipment and materials, preliminary design, specifications and quality assurance, cost and case histories.
sections.body: Deep dynamic compaction and vibro-compaction are mature, well-established methods of ground modification. The chapter provides an overview of the methods and presents the state of the practice in using them to improve site soils (p. 4-6). It addresses feasibility considerations (applications, advantages, limitations and potential disadvantages), construction equipment and required materials, preliminary design concepts, specification and quality assurance development, cost information, and case histories.
sections.applicability: Defines what the chapter covers for DDC and vibro-compaction.

sections.title: Alternative Technologies
sections.summary: Introduces other in situ compaction methods that densify cohesionless soils, some adding structural support: Frankipaction, blast densification, rapid impact compaction, compaction grouting and the vibratory hammer probe.
sections.body: A number of alternative methods of compacting ground in situ exist. Many of these techniques also densify cohesionless soils, with some adding structural support to the ground (p. 4-6). The manual lists five: Frankipaction, blast densification, rapid impact compaction, compaction grouting and the vibratory hammer probe, each described in the subsections that follow.
sections.applicability: Screening other densification technologies against DDC and VC.

sections.title: Frankipaction
sections.summary: Frankipaction adapts the driven, enlarged-base Franki pile: sand or gravel instead of concrete is driven by a drop hammer to form a compaction pile, placing large stone volumes in soft layers while densifying granular layers.
sections.body: The Frankipaction system is an adaptation of the Franki pile, a driven, enlarged-base pile, to achieve compaction. In the Franki pile a casing is set on the ground, a charge of dry concrete is placed in its bottom and driven by a drop hammer to form a dense plug that penetrates the ground dragging the casing with it; at depth the plug is driven down and outward to form the base, and successive charges are compacted as the casing is withdrawn to form the shaft. In Frankipaction sand or gravel is used instead of concrete, creating a compaction pile (p. 4-6). Its major advantage is the ability to put large volumes of stone in layers of soft or compressible soils to minimize settlements or potential shear failures of those layers, while still densifying the granular layers.
key_points: Sand or gravel replaces concrete in the Franki pile process to form a compaction pile (p. 4-6).
Puts large stone volumes into soft or compressible layers while densifying granular layers.
sections.applicability: Layered sites with soft compressible layers between granular layers.

sections.title: Blast Densification
sections.summary: Blast densification, used since the mid-1950s, is potentially economical but generally useful only for large areas and great depths (>100 ft); it can harm the natural and man-made environment, is prone to litigation, and needs high expertise.
sections.body: Blast densification has been used since the mid-1950s. Although potentially economical compared with other systems, it is generally only useful where densification is needed over large areas and at great depths (>100 ft) (p. 4-6). It has an inherent potential for negative effects on the natural and man-made environment, is more vulnerable to litigation than most other densification techniques, and therefore requires a high degree of expertise and experience. It is still useful under the right circumstances; a state DOT has reported densifying potentially liquefiable, loose volcanic debris avalanche deposits by blasting (Kimmerling 1994) (p. 4-7).
key_points: Generally useful only for large areas and depths greater than 100 ft (p. 4-6).
Potential environmental harm and litigation risk; requires high expertise.
sections.applicability: Very large, very deep densification where blasting risks can be managed.

sections.title: Rapid Impact Compaction
sections.summary: Rapid impact compaction drops a 5 to 9 ton excavator-mounted weight about 4 ft onto a 5 ft diameter tamper at 40 to 60 blows per minute, densifying to 10 to 20 ft depending on energy, soil and groundwater.
sections.body: Rapid impact compaction (RIC) uses a 5 to 9 ton excavator-mounted weight dropped about 4 ft onto a 5-foot diameter tamper, capable of 40 to 60 blows per minute. The resulting force densifies soils to depths of up to 10 to 20 ft. The depth of compaction depends on the compaction energy level, soil properties and groundwater conditions (p. 4-7).
key_points: Weight 5 to 9 tons, drop about 4 ft, 5 ft diameter tamper, 40 to 60 blows/min (p. 4-7).
Densifies to depths of up to 10 to 20 ft.
sections.applicability: Shallower densification (to about 10 to 20 ft) with excavator-mounted equipment.

sections.title: Compaction Grouting
sections.summary: Compaction grouting densifies weak, fractured or settled soil with a thick low-slump grout bulb that displaces soil; relatively new as a densification tool, possibly economical in finer grained or layered soils or where only localized layers at depth need treatment.
sections.body: Compaction grouting densifies cohesionless or weak soil, soil with fractures and air pockets, or soil that has settled, using a thick, low-slump grout that forms a bulb at the tip of the grout pipe and displaces the soil, compacting and strengthening the soil between bulbs; applications are described in Chapter 8, Grouting (p. 4-7). Its use as a densification tool is relatively new. Vibro-compaction and DDC are significantly more economical in granular soils, but compaction grouting might prove economical in finer grained or layered soils where strength gain is needed, and has economic advantages where only localized layers at depth need treatment.
key_points: DDC and VC are significantly more economical in granular soils (p. 4-7).
Compaction grouting can be economical in finer grained or layered soils, or for localized layers at depth.
sections.applicability: Localized deep layers or finer grained soils where DDC or VC are unsuitable.

sections.title: Vibratory Hammer Probe
sections.summary: The vibratory hammer probe transmits vibration vertically down a pipe about 2.6 ft in diameter, unlike vibro-compaction's horizontal vibration reaching up to 13 ft; it is less effective, needs much closer spacing and usually costs more overall.
sections.body: The vibratory hammer probe differs from vibro-compaction in that the vibrations are transmitted vertically down the attached pipe, typically 2.6 ft in diameter, whereas vibro-compaction transmits a horizontal vibration over a distance of up to 13 ft. The frequency of vibration and the location of the vibrator make it a less effective densification process, so it must be used on significantly closer pattern spacing, which usually results in higher overall cost (p. 4-7).
key_points: Vertical vibration down a pipe about 2.6 ft in diameter (p. 4-7).
Vibro-compaction transmits horizontal vibration up to 13 ft.
Requires significantly closer spacing; usually higher overall cost.
sections.applicability: Comparing top-driven vibratory probes with depth-vibrator vibro-compaction.

sections.title: Alternative Solutions
sections.summary: Before choosing densification, compare time and cost of alternatives: deep foundations (with a structural slab or reinforced stone mat for embankments), excavation and replacement, preloading (6 months to a year, wick drains), vibro-replacement, and deep soil stabilization such as jet grouting, deep soil mixing or compaction grouting.
sections.body: Before deciding on ground improvement by densification, alternate foundation solutions should be investigated to compare construction time and cost (p. 4-7). Besides relocating the project, common alternatives are: piles or drilled shafts transferring loads deeper, possibly with a structural slab or a geosynthetic-reinforced thick crushed-stone mat to transfer embankment loads (Chapter 6); excavation and replacement of weak ground, which may need sheeting and bracing or dewatering, and can be very costly where contaminated spoil must go to a special waste site; preloading to increase strength and reduce compressibility, which frequently causes delays of 6 months to one year, can be accelerated with wick drains, and may require importing and later removing surcharge (Chapter 2); vibro-replacement to stiffen clayey soils (Chapter 5); and deep soil stabilization such as jet grouting, deep soil mixing or compaction grouting (Chapters 7 and 8) (p. 4-8).
key_points: Deep foundations may need a structural slab or geosynthetic-reinforced stone mat under embankments (p. 4-8).
Preloading frequently delays a project 6 months to one year; wick drains accelerate it.
Contaminated spoil can make excavation and replacement very costly.
sections.applicability: Comparing densification against other foundation and ground improvement solutions.

sections.title: Liquefaction Potential and Mitigation Assessment
sections.summary: Mitigating liquefaction with DDC or VC: densify and/or contain loose sand; treat to the bottom of the liquefiable layer and laterally a distance equal to the treatment depth (Cooke and Mitchell 1999); compare CRR from SPT/CPT/BPT charts (Figure 4-3) with CSR; design to CRR/CSR greater than 1.5, minimum 1.3.
sections.body: Identifying liquefiable soils is beyond the manual's scope; typically they are loose natural or man-made sand deposits, and the chief strategy is to increase their density and/or contain them (p. 4-8). For highway structures and embankments Cooke and Mitchell (1999) recommend: improvement should extend to the bottom of the liquefiable material and laterally a distance equal to the depth of treatment; for reducing lateral deformation of embankments, treatment between crest and toe is more effective; and effects on structures are minor when the ground is improved to the no-liquefaction side of the simplified-method curves. Saturated sands, silty sands, sandy silts and silts are likely susceptible. The initial assessment compares the cyclic resistance ratio (CRR), the in situ cyclic strength, with the cyclic stress ratio (CSR). CRR is read from case-history boundary curves of CSR versus corrected penetration resistance or shear wave velocity from SPT, CPT or Becker tests (BPT) (Figure 4-3, Youd et al. 2001) (p. 4-9). Example: saturated clean sand with (N1)60 = 10 blows/ft and design CSR = 0.25 will liquefy unless (N1)60 is raised above 22 blows/ft by densification or the CSR is reduced by reinforcing elements; penetration resistance is normalized to 1 atmosphere effective overburden (p. 4-10). The analysis is complex because CSR depends on ground motions, CRR on overburden stress, fines content and static shear, and normalization needs several corrections. Ground motions may come from local records or USGS hazard tools; correlation charts and computations are in Youd et al. (2001) and Idriss and Boulanger (2008). The usual design requires densification to a factor of safety against triggering, CRR/CSR, greater than 1.5 with a minimum of 1.3, though no single value suits all conditions; scattered low points matter less than grouped ones, and large failures more than small. Earthquake settlement can be estimated per GEC 3 (1997) (p. 4-11).
key_points: Treat to the bottom of the liquefiable layer and laterally a distance equal to the treatment depth (Cooke and Mitchell 1999) (p. 4-8).
For embankments, treating between crest and toe is more effective against lateral deformation.
Example: (N1)60 = 10 with CSR = 0.25 liquefies unless (N1)60 is raised above 22 blows/ft (p. 4-10).
Usual design: factor of safety CRR/CSR greater than 1.5, minimum 1.3 (p. 4-10).
Several closely grouped low values are more significant than a few scattered ones (p. 4-11).
figures: Figure 4-3: SPT liquefaction chart for magnitude 7.5 earthquakes.
sections.applicability: Setting densification targets for DDC or VC to mitigate earthquake liquefaction.

sections.title: Glossary
sections.summary: Container heading for the glossary of terms unique to deep dynamic compaction (energy, crater, pass, phase) and to vibro-compaction (vibroflotation, vibro-displacement, vibro-replacement) (pp. 4-11 to 4-12).
sections.body: This heading introduces two short glossaries defining the terms unique to deep dynamic compaction (applied energy, contact pressure, crater, depth of improvement, drop energy, pass, phase and others) and to vibro-compaction (vibro-compaction, vibro-displacement, vibroflotation, vibro-replacement).
sections.applicability: Terminology used throughout the chapter.

sections.title: Deep Dynamic Compaction
sections.summary: Defines DDC terms: applied energy (total energy divided by treated area), contact pressure, crater, depth of improvement, drop energy (tamper mass times drop height), high- and low-level energy (ironing pass), induced settlement, pass and phase.
sections.body: Applied energy: average energy at the ground surface, the sum of all DDC energy divided by the surface area densified. Contact pressure: tamper weight divided by its base area. Crater: depression at the drop point from energy application. Depth of improvement: maximum depth to which measurable improvement is attained. Drop energy: energy per blow, tamper mass multiplied by drop height. High-level energy: energy applied to densify to the depth of improvement. Induced settlement: average ground settlement from elevation readings before and after DDC. Low-level energy: energy applied to compact surface deposits to the depth of crater penetration after the high-level energy, frequently called the ironing pass (p. 4-11). Pass: application of a portion of the planned energy at a single drop point; if all drops cannot be applied at once because of deep craters or excess pore pressure, further passes follow after pore pressures dissipate or craters are filled, generally with a waiting period of at least a few days. Phase: the pattern in which energy is applied, e.g. every other grid point as Phase 1 and the intermediate points as Phase 2; projects have used from one to as many as five phases (p. 4-12).
key_points: Drop energy = tamper mass x drop height (p. 4-11).
Applied energy = sum of all energy / surface area densified.
Ironing pass = low-level energy compacting to crater depth.
Waiting period between passes is generally at least a few days.
Projects have used one to five phases (p. 4-12).
sections.applicability: Definitions needed to specify and calculate DDC energy.

sections.title: Vibro-compaction
sections.summary: Defines vibro-compaction terms: vibro-compaction, vibro-displacement (dry top or bottom feed, soil displaced by backfill), vibroflotation (horizontal-vibration vibroprobe, the original name) and vibro-replacement (wet top feed with jetting, soil washed out and replaced by backfill).
sections.body: Vibro-compaction: a ground modification technique using specially designed probe-type depth vibrators for in situ densification of loose sands and gravels. Vibro-displacement: the dry, top or bottom feed process, in which almost no in situ soil appears at the surface because it is displaced by the backfill. Vibroflotation: compaction by a vibroprobe (vibroflot) densifying with predominantly horizontal vibrations; the original name, used synonymously with vibro-compaction. Vibro-replacement: the wet, top-feed process in which jetting water aids penetration, part of the in situ soil is washed to the surface and is replaced by backfill (p. 4-12).
key_points: Vibroflotation is the original name and is used synonymously with vibro-compaction (p. 4-12).
Vibro-displacement is dry; vibro-replacement is wet with jetting.
sections.applicability: Definitions of vibro methods used in this and Chapter 5.

sections.title: Deep Dynamic Compaction
sections.summary: Part 2.0 (pp. 4-14 to 4-63) covers deep dynamic compaction: the questions to answer first (applications, advantages, suitable deposits, limitations, alternatives, cost) and then feasibility, construction, design, specifications, cost and two case histories.
sections.body: Before an in-depth evaluation of deep dynamic compaction at a site, the manual says a number of fundamental questions must be addressed: what the typical applications are; what the advantages and disadvantages are; what types of deposits can be improved; whether there are limitations or environmental considerations; whether there are alternate site improvement methods; and whether DDC is cost-effective compared to the alternatives (p. 4-14). The sections that follow answer these questions: feasibility considerations, construction and materials, design, construction specifications and quality assurance, cost information, and case histories.

sections.summary: Container heading for DDC feasibility: applications, advantages and potential disadvantages, feasibility evaluations (geotechnical, environmental, site) and limitations (vibration, lateral movement, flying debris, depth).
sections.body: This heading introduces the feasibility considerations for deep dynamic compaction: its applications, its advantages and potential disadvantages, the geotechnical, environmental and site evaluations of feasibility, and its limitations (p. 4-14).
sections.applicability: Deciding whether DDC suits a site before design.

sections.title: Applications
sections.summary: DDC densifies natural and fill deposits to raise bearing, cut settlement, collapse voids and collapsible soils, and mitigate liquefaction. Best on dry granular soils and saturated free-draining soils; not generally for PI greater than 8 at high saturation; dynamic replacement in weak saturated soils with craters over 5 ft, improving less than about 10 to 13 ft.
sections.body: The primary purpose of DDC is to densify natural and fill deposits to increase bearing resistance, reduce settlement, minimize collapse of large voids or collapse-susceptible soils, and mitigate liquefaction so that bridges, abutments, retaining structures and embankments can be built safely and economically (p. 4-14). Densification of loose deposits (2.1.1.1): deposits include natural soils and fills of soil, debris and byproducts; DDC works best on dry granular materials (sands, gravels, ashes, mine spoils) and saturated free-draining soils. In partially saturated soils densification resembles Proctor impact compaction; in saturated fine sands and silts excess pore pressures develop on impact and, after dissipation, grains rearrange to a denser state (p. 4-15). In seismic areas DDC liquefies saturated sand or silty sand, leaving it denser and less susceptible to liquefaction. In fine-grained soils DDC can collapse air voids at low saturation and works best where water content is below the plastic limit; it is generally not recommended where PI is greater than 8 with high saturation; heave often occurs. Figure 4-4 shows successive phases expelling gas and liquid, lowering void ratio while solids stay constant (p. 4-16). Collapse of large voids and collapse-susceptible soils (2.1.1.2): voids in karst, in fills of construction debris, waste or mine spoil, or from buried drums and pipes can be collapsed if within the effective depth of treatment; DDC also overcomes weak cementation in loess and arid soils subject to collapse on wetting (p. 4-17). Related applications (2.1.1.3): in weak saturated soils craters greater than 5 ft can form; filling them with coarse granular material and applying more energy drives it into the deposit, called dynamic replacement, with improvement generally less than about 10 to 13 ft.
key_points: Works best on dry granular materials and saturated, free-draining soils (p. 4-14).
Works best where water content is below the plastic limit; generally not recommended for PI greater than 8 with high saturation (p. 4-15).
Voids must lie within the effective depth of treatment to be collapsed (p. 4-16).
Collapses weakly cemented loess and arid soils susceptible to collapse on wetting (p. 4-17).
Dynamic replacement: weak saturated soils with craters greater than 5 ft; improvement generally less than about 10 to 13 ft (p. 4-17).
figures: Figure 4-4: Phase diagram model of soil behavior during deep dynamic compaction.
sections.applicability: Identifying problems DDC can solve: loose deposits, voids, collapsible soils, liquefiable sands.

sections.title: Advantages and Potential Disadvantages
sections.summary: DDC advantages: the tamper probes and corrects; progress is visible in crater depths and induced settlement (5 to 10 percent of treatment depth, 20 to 25 percent in loose landfills); handles heterogeneous deposits; works below water in pervious soils. Disadvantages: vibration, water table under 6 ft, working mats, lateral movement of 1 to 3 in at about 20 ft.
sections.body: Advantages (2.1.2.1): impacting the tamper both probes and corrects, since weak zones or voids give deeper craters, giving immediate feedback to apply more energy or undercut, important in old landfills, mine spoils and karst (p. 4-17); densification can be observed, as each succeeding pass generally gives a smaller average crater depth, and ground compression normally equals 5 to 10 percent of the treatment depth predicted by Eq. 4-1, or 20 to 25 percent in extremely loose fills such as recent landfills; very heterogeneous deposits from boulders and broken concrete to silt, including building rubble and decomposed sanitary landfills, can be compacted with the same equipment; the bearing stratum becomes more uniform, minimizing differential settlement; densification below the water table in pervious and semi-pervious deposits avoids dewatering and bracing; except for very heavy tampers and high drops, non-specialty contractors can do the work, keeping cost competitive; work can continue in rain or freezing weather with precautions (p. 4-18). Potential disadvantages (2.1.2.2): ground vibrations may travel far, requiring lighter tampers, lower drops or work well inside property lines, and sometimes isolation trenches; the water table should be more than 6 ft below the surface to avoid softening and tamper sticking, or be lowered or the grade raised; very loose sites such as recent landfills often need a granular working layer, which adds cost; and lateral displacements of 1 to 3 inches have been measured about 20 ft from impacts of 30 to 60 kip tampers, so utilities and buried vessels may be displaced or damaged (p. 4-19).
key_points: Ground compression normally 5 to 10 percent of treatment depth (Eq. 4-1); 20 to 25 percent in extremely loose fills such as recent landfills (p. 4-18).
Succeeding passes give smaller average crater depths, showing improvement.
Water table should be more than 6 ft below the ground surface (p. 4-19).
Lateral displacements of 1 to 3 in measured about 20 ft from 30 to 60 kip tamper impacts (p. 4-19).
Heavier tampers and higher drops need modified equipment and specialty contractors.
sections.applicability: Weighing DDC's benefits against its vibration, groundwater and working-surface constraints.

sections.title: Feasibility Evaluations
sections.summary: Container heading for DDC feasibility evaluations: geotechnical suitability by soil grouping (Figure 4-5), environmental considerations, and site conditions (pp. 4-19 to 4-23).
sections.body: This heading introduces three evaluations of DDC feasibility: geotechnical (permeability, saturation, drainage path, stratigraphy and the soil grouping of Figure 4-5), environmental (noise, vibration, lateral movement, airborne debris), and site conditions (working surface, headroom, obstructions, depth).
sections.applicability: Structured feasibility screening for DDC.

sections.title: Geotechnical
sections.summary: DDC suitability depends on permeability, degree of saturation, drainage path length and stratigraphy. Figure 4-5 groups soils: Zone 1 pervious (k greater than 1e-5 m/s) best suited; Zone 2 semi-pervious (1e-5 to 1e-8 m/s) works if energy is applied in phases; Zone 3 impervious clayey (less than 1e-8 m/s) not recommended when saturated. Test sections help on variable sites.
sections.body: Suitability is evaluated from permeability (inferred from classification), degree of saturation (related to the water table), length of drainage path and stratigraphy such as buried hard or weak layers (p. 4-19). DDC works best where saturation is low, permeability high and drainage good. Pervious granular soils (natural sands and gravels, building rubble, granular mine spoil, some slags, decomposed refuse) densify immediately above the water table, and below it excess pore pressures dissipate almost immediately (p. 4-20). Saturated clayey soils are not appropriate: pore pressures take too long to dissipate and improvement is minor; their upper portion can be improved by dynamic replacement. Semi-pervious silts, clayey silts and sandy silts can be densified if energy is applied in multiple phases, with dissipation sometimes taking days to weeks; wick drains have been used to shorten the drainage path. Figure 4-5 (GEC 1 1995 after FHWA 1986) groups soils by gradation (p. 4-21): Zone 1, pervious, best suited, permeability generally greater than 10^-5 m/s, improved whether partially or fully saturated; Zone 3, impervious clayey, generally less than 10^-8 m/s, not recommended if saturated or nearly so, though partially saturated clayey fills have improved at water contents at or below the plastic limit; Zone 2, intermediate, generally 10^-5 to 10^-8 m/s, improved if energy is applied in multiple phases allowing complete pore pressure dissipation (p. 4-22). Procedure: plot the gradation on Figure 4-5; Zone 1, proceed; Zones 2 or 3, test water content and specific gravity for saturation, locate the water table and pervious seams, and consider field permeability testing, since field permeability, not gradation, dictates suitability; confirmed Zone 3, consider other methods; Zone 2, apply energy in phases. Test sections (SPT, CPT or PMT before and after; piezometers in fine soils) help on variable sites.
key_points: Zone 1 (pervious): k generally greater than 10^-5 m/s; best suited; works partially or fully saturated (p. 4-21).
Zone 2 (intermediate): k generally 10^-5 to 10^-8 m/s; works with energy in multiple phases (p. 4-22).
Zone 3 (impervious clayey): k generally less than 10^-8 m/s; not recommended if saturated; partially saturated clay fills at or below the plastic limit have improved (p. 4-21).
Field permeability, not grain size gradation, dictates suitability (p. 4-22).
Test sections with SPT, CPT or PMT before and after energy are valuable where stratigraphy varies.

sections.title: Environmental Considerations
sections.summary: Key DDC environmental concerns are noise (100 to 120 dB at 40 ft, under 80 dB at 80 ft on an open site), ground vibration travelling offsite, lateral ground displacement next to craters, and airborne debris.
sections.body: The key environmental considerations are noise, vibrations and lateral movements, which can affect neighboring structures and people. Typical noise levels on an open site can reach 100 to 120 dB at 40 ft, decreasing to less than 80 dB at 80 ft (Dumas and Beaton 1992); noise normally occurs only during short periods of the lifting and dropping cycle. Ground vibrations can travel significant distances offsite to nearby property and structures (vibration analysis is in Section 2.1.4). Lateral ground displacement adjacent to craters may damage existing utilities and structures, and airborne debris can cause damage or injury unless precautions are taken (p. 4-22).
key_points: Noise 100 to 120 dB at 40 ft, decreasing to less than 80 dB at 80 ft on an open site (Dumas and Beaton 1992) (p. 4-22).
Lateral displacement next to craters may damage utilities and structures.
sections.applicability: Assessing noise, vibration, displacement and debris impacts of DDC on neighbors.

sections.title: Site Conditions
sections.summary: Site conditions affecting DDC economics and feasibility: an uneven or unstable working surface (needs a free-draining working layer), headroom and overhead lines (must be de-energized), near-surface obstructions that absorb energy, and depth (improvement 10 to 35 ft; deeper needs combined methods).
sections.body: DDC needs headroom for the cranes, and adjacent buildings, structures, utilities and property must be monitored for vibration, noise and lateral movement. The site investigation should establish soil types, densities and water contents, groundwater level, and overhead wires, buried utilities or nearby structures (p. 4-23). Conditions affecting economics or feasibility: an uneven, unstable working surface, since cranes need a level stable surface, so a working layer, best of free-draining material and able to carry the cranes, may be placed; headroom, since overhead lines must be de-energized to avoid impact or arcing to the mast; obstructions above the compressible layer (concrete, rock, rubble, slag, brick, wood, riprap, debris) that reduce the energy reaching the compressible layer, so more drops may be needed; and depth, as soil is improved to between 10 and 35 ft, and deeper improvement calls for DDC combined with other systems such as grouting and stone columns. Where these conditions occur, specialty DDC contractors should be consulted.
key_points: Overhead lines must be de-energized (p. 4-23).
Near-surface obstructions reduce energy reaching the compressible layer; more drops may be needed.
Improvement depth 10 to 35 ft; deeper needs DDC combined with grouting or stone columns.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.summary: DDC limits: vibration (frequencies 5 to 12 Hz; limit peak particle velocity to 1/2 in/s for plaster and 3/4 in/s for drywall; predict with the scaled energy factor, Figure 4-7); lateral movement (10 to 12 in at 10 ft, 1/2 to 3 in at 20 ft; stay about 23 to 26 ft from buried structures for 33 to 66 kip tampers); flying debris; cable wear; maximum depth about 36 ft.
sections.body: Vibrations diminish with distance from impact, so DDC near property lines must consider offsite vibration. There are no general regulations for construction vibration; the U.S. Bureau of Mines related building damage to particle velocity (Siskind et al. 1980) and developed Figure 4-6 from blast-induced damage in residences (p. 4-24). DDC normally gives frequencies of 5 to 12 Hz, which by Figure 4-6 limits peak particle velocity to 1/2 inch/sec for older residences with plaster walls and 3/4 inch/sec for modern drywall construction; these are lower thresholds for cracking, not damage limits. Minor damage occurs above 2 inch/sec and major damage above about 7.6 inch/sec, so keeping particle velocity below about 1/2 to 3/4 inch/sec is reasonably conservative (p. 4-25). Before work, predict particle velocity with Figure 4-7: the scaled energy factor is the square root of the single-drop energy (drop height times tamper mass) divided by the distance from impact, read with the closest soil type (p. 4-26). If too high, reduce energy or increase distance; property-line trenches were partially helpful. People find 1/2 to 3/4 inch/sec (13 to 19 mm/sec) disturbing. Buried utilities tolerate more; water mains have sustained 3 inch/sec without damage. Inclinometers 3 m and 6 m (10 and 20 ft) from impacts of 15-29 Mg (33-64 kip) tampers in three soil types (Figures 4-8, 4-9) showed lateral deformations of 254 to 305 mm (10 to 12 in) at 3 m and 13 to 76 mm (1/2 to 3 in) at 6 m, permanent; so DDC with 15-30 Mg (33-66 kip) tampers should not be done within about 6 to 7 m (23 to 26 ft) of buried structures that movement could damage (p. 4-28). Airborne debris needs a safe working distance and possibly a shield; cable wear needs swivels, shorter cables, tag lines, non-rotating cables or similar (FHWA 1986). The heaviest tamper conventional equipment lifts is about 40 kips at 75 to 90 ft, giving a maximum improvement depth of about 36 ft; deeper needs combined methods.

sections.title: Construction and Materials
sections.summary: Container heading for DDC construction and materials: equipment overview, tampers, lifting equipment, surface stabilizing layer, and construction sequencing (pp. 4-28 to 4-38).
sections.body: This heading introduces the equipment and materials used for deep dynamic compaction and how the work is sequenced: an overview, tampers, lifting equipment, the surface stabilizing layer, and construction sequencing in phases and passes.
sections.applicability: Equipment and construction aspects of DDC.

sections.title: Overview
sections.summary: Conventional lifting cranes are used where the tamper is under about 40 kips; tampers may be purpose-built or improvised; a dozer levels craters and imported granular fill may form a working mat; many general contractors can do DDC when properly guided and monitored.
sections.body: Conventional lifting cranes are used for DDC where the tamper is less than about 40 kips. Tampers are sometimes built especially for DDC, while others have been fashioned from steel ingots or other sources such as a bank vault door (p. 4-28). Associated equipment includes a front-end dozer for leveling the ground after the craters are formed, and imported granular material may be needed for a firm working mat. Because the equipment is conventional and readily available, many general, demolition or excavation contractors will perform DDC when properly guided and monitored (p. 4-29).
key_points: Conventional cranes for tampers under about 40 kips (p. 4-28).
General, demolition or excavation contractors can perform DDC when guided and monitored (p. 4-29).
sections.applicability: Planning DDC equipment and contractor pool.

sections.title: Tampers
sections.summary: DDC tampers range from 11 to 60 kips (lighter for about 10 ft deposits, heaviest for 30 to 40 ft). Rugged, mostly solid steel or steel shell filled with concrete; flat base, round, square or hexagonal. Contact pressure should be 5 to 10 psi; ironing-pass tampers 1.5 to 5 psi.
sections.body: DDC is generally performed with tampers from 11 to 60 kips: lighter tampers where the deposit is thin, such as 10 ft, and the heaviest where it is about 30 to 40 ft thick (p. 4-29). Tampers must be very rugged because of high impact stresses; most are solid steel, some have a steel base plate and sidewalls filled with concrete, and all-concrete tampers have a short life. They should have a flat base and may be square, round or hexagonal; because the cable unwinds and the tamper rotates as it is lifted, a round tamper always hits the same imprint, while square tampers produce a rounded crater; guy wires are sometimes used to stop rotation. Contact pressure (tamper weight divided by base area) should be 5 to 10 psi: much higher causes penetration without densification, and less than about 5 psi spreads energy too widely for deep densification. Figures 4-10 to 4-13 show 12, 30, 31 and 70 kip tampers; the 12 kip tamper has a round 6 inch thick steel base plate and a 1 inch thick steel cylinder filled with concrete, the 30 kip tamper has stacked welded and bolted steel plates on a base plate, and the 70 kip tamper is solid steel (p. 4-32). Low-contact-pressure tampers, typically 1.5 to 5 psi, are sometimes used for surface compaction afterward (Figure 4-14); surface densification may instead use conventional compaction equipment or proofrolling with a loaded dump truck.

sections.title: Lifting Equipment
sections.summary: Tampers are lifted and dropped by a single cable on a free-spool drum to deliver maximum energy; conventional crawler cranes serve 10 to 40 kip tampers (Table 4-1 gives crane and cable size); 35 to 50 kip tampers need modified rigs; specialized cranes or multiple-part-line rigs with release mechanisms serve 50 to 60 kip and heavier tampers.
sections.body: To deliver maximum energy the tamper is lifted and dropped with a single cable on a free-spool drum; the only losses are free-spool drum friction, cable friction over the upper boom sheave, and some air resistance at the tamper base (p. 4-32). Typical equipment is shown in Figures 4-15 to 4-17. Specialized equipment may raise the tamper on multiple-part lines and then release it to free fall, also acceptable (p. 4-34). Conventional lifting cranes generally handle 10 to 40 kip tampers; Table 4-1 gives crawler crane size and cable size: 8 to 16 kip tamper, 80 to 100 kip crane, 3/4 to 7/8 inch cable; 16 to 28 kips, 100 to 200 kips, 7/8 to 1 inch; 30 to 36 kips, 200 to 250 kips, 1 to 1-1/8 inch; 36 to 50 kips, 300 to 350 kips, 1-1/4 to 1-1/2 inch. For 35 to 50 kip tampers conventional equipment must be modified: release causes rocking that stresses the shaft connecting cab to tracks, so spuds reduce rocking and lifting drums are enlarged and thickened. Specialized lifting equipment has been devised for 50-60 kip tampers (p. 4-35); one crane built only for DDC (Figure 4-18) has a lifting drum about 5 ft in diameter and an upper carriage fixed to the tracks, which protects the cab-track connection but makes maneuvering harder. Figure 4-19 shows multiple part lines lifting a 64 kip tamper for free fall.

sections.title: Surface Stabilizing Layer
sections.summary: On soft ground (recent landfills with thin cover, mine spoil weathered to soft clay) a granular stabilizing layer, typically 6 inch maximum size down to sand, 1 to 3 ft thick, carries equipment and limits tamper penetration; it can cost as much as the DDC, so it is used only where absolutely necessary.
sections.body: Where soft ground prevails a surface stabilizing layer may be needed so the DDC equipment can travel across the site and to reduce tamper penetration. Soft deposits include fairly recent landfills with a thin cover, or mine spoil weathered to a softer clay consistency at the surface (p. 4-36). The layer usually consists of granular material graded from 6 inch maximum size down to sand size; thicknesses of 1 to 3 ft have been used successfully, depending on the stability of the surface deposits. Figure 4-20 shows DDC over 3 ft of crushed rock placed on a landfill. Where deposits are more stable, such as building rubble, loose granular outwash, or old decomposed landfills above the water table, no stabilizing layer is needed. Because the layer can cost as much as the DDC itself, it is used only where absolutely necessary (p. 4-37).
key_points: Granular, 6 inch maximum size down to sand; 1 to 3 ft thick (p. 4-36).

sections.title: Construction Sequencing
sections.summary: DDC is applied on a grid over the whole area, extending beyond it a distance equal to the weak deposit's thickness, in single or multiple phases (patterns, e.g. 25 ft centers then midpoints) and passes (drop increments at a point, e.g. 3 of 12 drops). Fine-grained deposits may need 3 or 4 passes; pervious ones 1.
sections.body: DDC is generally done on a grid over the entire project area and extends beyond the limits of the project a distance equal to the thickness of the weak deposit being densified (pp. 4-37 to 4-38). Energy can be applied in single or multiple phases and passes. A phase is application of energy in a specific pattern, e.g. Phase 1 on 25 ft centers and Phase 2 midway between initial points. A single phase is used where pore pressures dissipate rapidly and adjacent points can be treated at once; multiple phases are used where pore pressures rise and take time to dissipate, making an intermittent pattern more effective. A pass is application of energy in increments at a drop point: if 12 drops are planned but only 3 can be applied before craters become excessive or the ground heaves, those 3 are the first pass; pore pressures then dissipate, craters are filled, and further drops form the second pass. Fine-grained deposits sometimes need 3 or 4 passes; more pervious deposits need only 1 (p. 4-38). Additional energy may be applied at footing locations, or in karst where larger induced settlement signals voids.

sections.title: Design
sections.summary: Container heading for DDC design: design considerations, performance requirements, the design procedure (depth and degree of improvement by Eq. 4-1, energy requirements by Eq. 4-2 and Table 4-3), and a planning example (pp. 4-38 to 4-47).
sections.body: This heading introduces deep dynamic compaction design: the design considerations, performance requirements, the design procedure for depth and degree of improvement and for energy requirements, and a worked planning example.
sections.applicability: Designing a DDC program.

sections.title: Design Considerations
sections.summary: Once DDC is judged appropriate, the detailed plan determines the performance requirements, selects tamper mass and drop height for the required depth of improvement, estimates the degree of improvement, and sets the applied energy; details are in GEC 1 (1995).
sections.body: If the preliminary considerations indicate DDC is appropriate, the next step is a more specific or detailed plan of the DDC procedures (p. 4-38). The plan includes: determining the project performance requirements for the completed structure; selecting the tamper mass and drop height to correspond to the required depth of improvement; estimating the degree of improvement DDC will produce; and determining the applied energy over the site to produce that improvement (p. 4-39). The chapter is a brief summary of the design concepts; FHWA GEC 1 (1995) gives additional details.
key_points: Design steps: performance requirements; tamper mass and drop height for depth; degree of improvement; applied energy (pp. 4-38 to 4-39).
GEC 1 (1995) provides additional design detail.
sections.applicability: Organizing the steps of DDC design.

sections.title: Performance Requirements
sections.summary: Required soil properties (from SPT, CPT or PMT based analyses) are compared with estimated post-DDC properties; e.g. most embankments tolerate up to 6 in of uniform, slow settlement away from pile-supported structures (Holtz 1975). Similar checks apply to bearing and liquefaction; verification testing is required, and DDC reveals unforeseen loose pockets in uncontrolled fill.
sections.body: DDC densifies the soil, improving shear strength and reducing compressibility. The minimum property values needed for adequate performance are determined by conventional analysis, usually based on SPT, CPT or PMT, and compared with the estimated post-densification properties to judge whether DDC can produce the desired effect (p. 4-39). For a roadway embankment over weak ground, most embankments can withstand up to 6 inches of settlement without detrimental pavement performance, provided it is reasonably uniform, not next to a pile-supported structure, and very slow (Holtz 1975); a settlement prediction from the estimated densified properties shows whether settlement stays under 6 inches. Bearing capacity is checked the same way, and for liquefaction the minimum SPT or CPT values from the analysis are compared with the estimated post-DDC values. The estimates are made before the project, but verification of improvement by field testing is required (p. 4-40). In uncontrolled fills an extremely loose pocket missed by the borings will show up during grid compaction, and can be given additional energy or undercut and replaced with granular material that is then dynamically compacted.
key_points: Compare required property values with estimated post-DDC values from SPT, CPT or PMT (p. 4-39).
Most embankments tolerate up to 6 in of uniform, slow settlement not next to pile-supported structures (Holtz 1975) (p. 4-39).

sections.title: Design Procedure
sections.summary: Container heading for the DDC design procedure: depth and degree of improvement (Eq. 4-1, Figures 4-21 to 4-23, Table 4-2) and energy requirements (Eq. 4-2, Table 4-3) (pp. 4-40 to 4-46).
sections.body: This heading introduces the two parts of the DDC design procedure: estimating the depth and degree of improvement from tamper mass and drop height (Eq. 4-1) with upper-bound post-treatment test values (Table 4-2), and estimating the average applied energy (Eq. 4-2) with unit energy guidelines (Table 4-3) (p. 4-40).
sections.applicability: Calculating DDC depth of improvement and energy.

sections.title: Depth and Degree of Improvement
sections.summary: Eq. 4-1: D = n(WH)^(1/2), D in meters, W tamper mass in Mg, H drop height in m; n is approximately 0.5 for most soils, varies between 0.3 and 0.8 (Figure 4-21), and 0.4 is typically used for landfills. Improvement peaks at D/3 to D/2; Table 4-2 gives upper-bound SPT, CPT and PMT values after DDC; properties may improve further with time.
sections.body: Depth of improvement depends on tamper mass, drop height, soil type and average applied energy, accounted for by Eq. 4-1, D = n(WH)^(1/2), where D is depth of improvement in meters; n is an empirical coefficient approximately 0.5 for most soils, which as shown in Figure 4-21 varies between 0.3 and 0.8, with 0.4 typically used for landfills; W is tamper mass in megagrams (metric tonnes = 1.10 US ton); and H is drop height in meters (1 meter = 3.28 feet) (p. 4-40). Figure 4-21 (Mayne et al. 1984) plots maximum depth of influence against energy per blow WH (kJ) with lines Dmax = 0.3, 0.5 and 0.8(WH)^0.5. Soft energy-absorbing layers (low strength clay, organics) and hard surface layers reduce depth (FHWA 1986; Han 2015) (p. 4-41). Various W and H combinations may be used; Figure 4-22 summarizes those used on projects as a starting point (p. 4-42). Improvement is measured by SPT, CPT or PMT before and after, and is greatest in the upper part of the layer, decreasing with depth (Figure 4-23). Degree of improvement depends mainly on average applied energy, but there are upper limits (p. 4-43). Table 4-2 (FHWA 1986) gives upper-bound values, the maximum improvement at depths of D/3 to D/2, measured where average energy was typically 41,300-62,000 ft-lbf/ft2; less energy, energy-absorbing layers or a hard crust give less (p. 4-44). Table 4-2 is for estimating the maximum possible improvement; actual improvement must be measured, partly while equipment is on site. Delayed improvement occurs after pore pressures dissipate: Lukas (1997) reported SPT or PMT gains of 15 to 200 percent years later on 5 projects, and Schmertmann (1991) stated gains of 50 to 100 percent can occur, attributed to cementation, secondary consolidation and aging, mostly in fine-grained soils. Borderline results may be retested later (pp. 4-44 to 4-45).

sections.title: Energy Requirements
sections.summary: Eq. 4-2: AE = (W)(H)(N)(P)/(grid spacing)^2, average applied energy in tm/m2 from tamper mass, drop height, drops per point and passes; energies from different tampers add. Most projects used about 21,000 to 62,000 ft-lbf/ft2 (1 to 3 MJ/m2); Table 4-3 gives unit applied energy per volume by deposit type.
sections.body: Because DDC is done on a grid, applied energy is expressed as an average, by Eq. 4-2, AE = (W)(H)(N)(P)/(grid spacing)^2, where AE is applied energy in tm/m2 (9.76 tm/m2 = 1 TSF), N the number of drops at each drop point, W tamper mass in Mg (1 metric tonne = 1.10 US ton), H drop height in m, P the number of passes, and grid spacing in m (1 m = 3.28 ft). Useful conversions: 1 metric tonne = 9.807 kN = 1 Mg; 1 U.S. ton = 0.907 metric tonne; 1 tonne-meter/m2 = 9.807 kJ/m2 = 0.1024 TSF. Where different tampers and drop heights are used, such as a high-energy phase followed by an ironing pass with a smaller tamper and lower drop, the average applied energy is the sum. Most projects have used about 21,000 to 62,000 ft-lbf/ft2 (1 to 3 MJ/m2), varied to suit the improvement needed (p. 4-45). For initial planning, Table 4-3 gives unit applied energy per volume: pervious coarse-grained soil (Zone 1 of Figure 4-5) 4,100 to 5,200 ft-lbf/ft3 (200 to 250 kJ/m3), 33 to 41 percent of standard Proctor energy; semipervious fine-grained soils (Zone 2, and clay fills above the water table and Zone 3) 5,200 to 7,200 ft-lbf/ft3 (250 to 350 kJ/m3), 41 to 60 percent; landfills 12,400 to 22,700 ft-lbf/ft3 (600 to 1100 kJ/m3), 100 to 180 percent; standard Proctor energy equals 12,400 ft-lbf/ft3. The table reflects deposit thickness (energy per unit volume, multiplied by thickness to get surface energy), soil type and initial relative density, with the loosest deposits taking the upper value and denser ones the lower (p. 4-46).

sections.title: Example
sections.summary: Planning example: a loose rubble fill 26 ft thick (Zone 1) takes the upper Table 4-3 energy of 5,200 per foot of depth, giving about 41,000 ft-lbf/ft2; W and H come from Eq. 4-1, grid spacing is 1.5 to 2.5 tamper diameters, and Eq. 4-2 is solved for N x P, preferably P = 1.
sections.body: A site of loose rubble fill 26 ft thick is classed as pervious coarse-grained soil, Zone 1. Because it is loose, the upper-bound applied energy of 5,200 is used (printed as ft-lbf/ft2; Table 4-3 lists it per ft3), and for the 26 ft thickness 41,000 ft-lbf/ft2 of average applied energy is required (p. 4-46). Substituting into Eq. 4-2, with tamper mass and drop height from Eq. 4-1, combinations of drops, grid spacing and passes are evaluated. The grid spacing is usually 1.5 to 2.5 times the tamper diameter, and Eq. 4-2 is solved for N x P; applying all energy in one pass is more efficient for the contractor, so with P = 1 the number of drops per point follows. Multiple passes are used when not all drops can be made at once, with N x P unchanged (p. 4-47). Table 4-3 relates to standard Proctor energy (ASTM D698), printed as 12,400 ft-lbf/ft2: pervious coarse-grained soils need about 33 to 41 percent because of some natural densification after placement, while landfills, extremely loose and possibly underconsolidated, need 100 to 180 percent. Close monitoring with SPT, CPT or PMT during DDC should verify that the desired improvement is reached.
key_points: Loose 26 ft Zone 1 rubble fill: upper-bound unit energy 5,200 gives 41,000 ft-lbf/ft2 average applied energy (p. 4-46).
Grid spacing usually 1.5 to 2.5 times the tamper diameter (p. 4-47).
Solve Eq. 4-2 for N x P; one pass (P = 1) is most efficient.
The example prints the unit energy and Proctor energy in ft-lbf/ft2 although Table 4-3 lists them per ft3.
sections.applicability: Planning-level DDC energy and drop calculation.

sections.title: Construction Specifications and Quality Assurance
sections.summary: DDC is contracted by a method approach (designer sets tamper, drop, energy, passes, phases, working mat) or a performance approach (contractor achieves specified depth and degree of improvement); full specifications are in GEC 1 (1995) and GeoTechTools.
sections.body: The chapter briefly summarizes methods for contracting DDC and the monitoring that normally occurs during field work; complete construction specifications are in FHWA GEC 1 (1995), with more information in GeoTechTools (p. 4-47). The designer develops drawings and specifications that establish the basis of payment and the quality assurance program, using either a method approach or a performance approach, described in the subsections.
sections.applicability: Contracting and quality assurance for DDC.

sections.title: Contracting Procedures
sections.summary: Method specification: designer gives tamper mass and size, drop height, grid, energy, phases or passes, site preparation, surface compaction, drawings, subsurface data and any test section; owner monitors and tests. Performance specification: designer sets required depth and degree of improvement and end-product criteria; contractor selects procedures; only experienced contractors (about five to eight U.S. specialists) should bid; cost is generally higher.
sections.body: Under the method approach the designer outlines the work plan: tamper size, drop height, average energy, single or multiple passes or phases, working mat and all other facets needed (pp. 4-47 to 4-48). It is becoming more common as DDC knowledge spreads among designers, and allows general contractors to do some of the work. Under the performance approach the contractor is responsible for the result; the designer specifies the required depth and degree of improvement and site and soil information, and the contractor selects tamper, drop height and other specifics. Only experienced contractors should bid; there are about five to eight DDC specialty contractors in the United States, and because they do significant engineering and planning, costs are generally higher than under method specifications (p. 4-48). Method specification (2.4.1.1) items: tamper mass and size; drop height; grid spacing; applied energy; number of phases or passes; site preparation; surface compaction after DDC; drawings of the working area; subsurface investigation data; test section design if relevant. The owner or designer monitors construction and performs borings and tests after DDC; the contractor provides adequate equipment, ensures safety and provides a work plan for the designer's approval (p. 4-49). Performance specification (2.4.1.2) items: minimum soil property value and method of verification; maximum permissible settlement; other objectives; minimum contractor qualifications. The owner provides initial subsurface data and the lateral extent and does some monitoring; the contractor provides equipment and work plan, meets the deadline, ensures safety, monitors, performs any additional exploration and verifies the end product.
key_points: Method approach: designer specifies the procedure; more common; allows general contractors (p. 4-48).
Performance approach: contractor achieves the specified depth and degree of improvement; only experienced contractors; generally higher cost (p. 4-48).
About five to eight DDC specialty contractors in the United States (p. 4-48).
Method specification lists tamper mass and size, drop height, grid spacing, applied energy, phases or passes, site preparation, surface compaction, drawings, subsurface data, test section (p. 4-48).
Performance specification sets minimum property and verification method, maximum settlement, other objectives and contractor qualifications (p. 4-49).
sections.applicability: Choosing and writing a DDC method or performance specification.

sections.title: Instrumentation Monitoring and Construction Control
sections.summary: DDC monitoring: vibration readings near structures; crater depth and adjacent heave to find the useful number of drops; average induced subsidence (usually 5 to 10 percent, more in landfills); SPT, CPT or PMT during and after (load tests in landfills); piezometers in fine-grained soils; testing 30 to 60 days after completion.
sections.body: Whether under method or performance approach, DDC operations must be monitored, since the field program frequently needs adjusting (p. 4-50). Monitoring includes: vibration readings near structures, peak particle velocity being correlated with building damage; measuring crater depths and adjacent heave at occasional drop points to find the efficient number of drops, since after six or seven drops craters may deepen much less per drop and heave may begin, and when added crater volume equals adjacent heave no more compaction occurs; measuring average ground subsidence on a grid before and after, generally 5 to 10 percent except in landfills where it could be higher; field testing during DDC by borings with SPT, CPT or PMT, or in landfills where in situ testing is often meaningless, load tests with settlement readings over at least 1 week; piezometers below the water table in silts or clayey silts to set waiting periods between drops; and general observation, with extra tamping where subsidence is unusually large or longer waits or undercutting where heave is excessive (p. 4-51). After DDC, explorations with SPT, CPT or PMT confirm depth and degree of improvement; since values have improved 30 to 60 days after completion, testing then is helpful. Settlement plates and inclinometers are optional. Under a method specification the owner and designer monitor; under a performance specification the contractor monitors and tests, but owner field personnel are still advisable.
key_points: Additional drops stop producing compaction when crater volume equals adjacent heave (p. 4-50).
Craters may deepen much less per drop after six or seven drops (p. 4-50).
Average induced subsidence generally 5 to 10 percent, higher in landfills (p. 4-50).
In landfills, load tests with settlement readings over at least 1 week (p. 4-50).
Post-DDC SPT, CPT and PMT values have improved 30 to 60 days after completion (p. 4-51).
sections.applicability: Field control and verification of DDC.

sections.title: Cost Information
sections.summary: Container heading for deep dynamic compaction cost: unit cost components by tamper size (Table 4-4) and cost data with the additional planning cost factors such as working mats and fill (pp. 4-52 to 4-53).
sections.body: This heading introduces deep dynamic compaction cost information: the cost components, which vary with depth of improvement and hence tamper size (Table 4-4), and cost data with the other cost factors to include in planning.
sections.applicability: Budgeting DDC.

sections.title: Cost Components
sections.summary: DDC cost rises with depth of improvement (heavier tamper, higher drop, bigger crane); predictable up to 40 kip tampers. Table 4-4 unit costs: 4 to 8 kips $1.10 to 1.50/ft2; 8 to 16 kips $1.50 to 2.00/ft2; 16 to 20 kips $2.00 to 3.00/ft2; 20 to 90 kips negotiated for each job.
sections.body: The cost of DDC varies with the depth of improvement required, since greater depth needs a heavier tamper, higher drop and a much heavier lifting crane. For tampers up to 40 kips, costs are relatively predictable because conventional lifting equipment can be used. Table 4-4 compares cost with tamper size: 4 to 8 kips, $1.10 to 1.50 per ft2; 8 to 16 kips, $1.50 to 2.00 per ft2; 16 to 20 kips, $2.00 to 3.00 per ft2; 20 to 90 kips, negotiated for each job. These costs include mobilization for large projects; on small projects mobilization should be added. They exclude the quality assurance program and any granular fill to fill craters or form a surface stabilizing layer (p. 4-52).
key_points: Costs include mobilization for large projects; add it for small projects.
Costs exclude QA and granular fill for craters or a stabilizing layer.
sections.applicability: Planning-level DDC unit cost by tamper size.

sections.title: Cost Data
sections.summary: DDC costs vary with location, deposit and local contractors: under about 15 to 20 kips many earthwork contractors can do it, 20 to 40 kips mostly specialists, over 35 to 40 kips specialized equipment and much higher cost. Plan by depth, Eq. 4-1, drop height, then Table 4-4; add working platform, fill for 5 to 10 percent induced settlement, undercutting and testing.
sections.body: Costs vary considerably with geographic location, deposit type and availability of local contractors. For tampers lighter than about 15 to 20 kips many excavating and earthmoving contractors have adequate equipment; for 20 to 40 kips heavier lifting equipment is needed and much of the work is done by specialty contractors. Above 35 to 40 kips specialized equipment is necessary, such as a crane modified with a large-diameter hoist (Figure 4-17, 64 kip tamper) or a specialized crane for 64 to 100 kip tampers (Figure 4-18), at much higher cost (p. 4-52). For planning, select the desired depth, use Eq. 4-1 to predict the proper energy, select a drop height, find the tamper mass, and estimate cost from Table 4-4; more in GEC 1 (1995) and GeoTechTools. Other cost factors: a working platform over soft ground; additional fill to maintain grade; undercutting of weak deposits such as Zone 3 soils that do not respond; and trial test sections and pre- and post-construction monitoring and testing. On weak deposits such as landfills 1 to 3 ft of crushed rock or granular material may be imported, and where grade must be kept, fill must make up induced settlement that could be 5 to 10 percent of the densified thickness (p. 4-53).
key_points: Tampers under about 15 to 20 kips: many earthwork contractors; 20 to 40 kips: mostly specialty contractors (p. 4-52).
Above 35 to 40 kips specialized equipment and much higher costs.
Plan: depth, Eq. 4-1, drop height, tamper mass, then Table 4-4 (p. 4-53).
Landfills may need 1 to 3 ft of imported crushed rock or granular material.
Fill to maintain grade may equal 5 to 10 percent of the densified thickness (p. 4-53).
sections.applicability: Estimating DDC cost and its additional cost items.

sections.title: Case Histories
sections.summary: The manual presents two DDC case histories to illustrate typical applications: a highway embankment built over mine spoil and a highway embankment on old landfill debris.
sections.body: Two case histories are presented to illustrate typical applications of deep dynamic compaction: a highway built over recent mine spoil, and a highway bypass embankment crossing two areas of old landfill refuse. Each follows the chapter's design procedure (Eq. 4-1, Table 4-3 and Eq. 4-2) for the predicted densification and compares it with what was actually done, the improvement measured, and the contracting procedure and cost (p. 4-53).
sections.applicability: Worked DDC applications in transportation projects.

sections.title: Highway Embankment Constructed in Mine Spoil
sections.summary: Manual's case history: an interstate over about 2,500 ft of recent mine spoil (50 to 120 ft deep, about 50 percent over 2 in, SPT mostly 15-20). Design: D = 9 m, n = 0.5 gives WH = 324; 20 Mg tamper, 16.5 m drop; 250 kJ/m3 gives 2250 kJ/m2; 3 m grid gives about 6 drops. Actual: 19 m drop, 5 drops, ironing pass; improvement to about 35 ft; cost about $7.20/m2.
sections.body: This is the manual's first DDC case history. An interstate was extended about 2,500 ft over a mine spoil area; final grade needed about 15 ft of fill at the ends and a 45 ft cut in the center, leaving 50 to 120 ft of spoil below a 182 ft wide roadway (p. 4-53). The spoil, rock fragments in a silt-sand matrix with about 50 percent larger than 2 inches, was recent. SPT values were mostly 15-20 blows/ft, some 5-10 and some 25-35 (Figure 4-24); groundwater was over 100 ft deep (p. 4-54). Goals: a uniform subgrade, crushing deteriorating rock, and densifying loose zones in the upper 25 to 30 ft; DDC was much cheaper than excavating and recompacting 25 ft (p. 4-55). Predicted procedure: D = 30 ft (9 m), n = 0.5, Eq. 4-1 gives 9 = 0.5(WH)^1/2, WH = 324; from Figure 4-22 with W = 20 Mg (44 kip), H 15 to 31 m, use H = 16.5 m (WH = 330). Table 4-3 Zone 2, medium dense: E = 250 kJ/m3, times 9 m = 2250 kJ/m2. With a 2 m tamper, 3 m grid, one pass plus a 250 kJ/m2 ironing pass, Eq. 4-2 gives (2250 - 250) = (20)(10)(16.5)(N)/(3)^2, N = 5.5, six drops (pp. 4-55 to 4-56). Table 4-2 maximum SPT 25-35 (sandy silts) and 20-35 (clayey silts); induced settlement 5 percent of 9 m = 0.45 m. Actual: from a test section, 20 Mg tamper, 19 m drop, five drops on a 3.0 m grid, then an ironing pass with 5.8 m drop, 1.8 m grid, one drop: 2.1 MJ/m2 plus 0.36 MJ/m2, about as calculated (p. 4-56). Improvement reached about 10.7 m (35 ft) (Figure 4-25); subsidence about 0.6 m on test pads and 0.5 m in production; crater depths normally 1 to 1.1 m, 1.5 to 2.7 m in soft or void areas that got extra tamping (Figure 4-26) (p. 4-58). A method specification let an excavating contractor do 37,200 m2 in 100 working days (372 m2/day; 63 and 67 impacts/hour). Bids were $2.90 and $2.65 per drop, about $7.20 per m2 ($6.00 per yd2), about 4 percent of project cost; excavation and recompaction of 6.1 m would have cost about 2.6 times as much (p. 4-59).

Table 4-3 Zone 2 energy 250 kJ/m3 x 9 m = 2250 kJ/m2 (p. 4-55).
Eq. 4-2 on a 3 m grid gave N = 5.5, six drops per point (p. 4-56).
Actual: 20 Mg tamper, 19 m drop, 5 drops at 3.0 m; ironing pass 5.8 m drop, 1.8 m grid; 2.1 + 0.36 MJ/m2 (p. 4-56).
Improvement observed to about 10.7 m (35 ft) (p. 4-56).
Production subsidence 0.5 m; normal craters 1 to 1.1 m, 1.5 to 2.7 m in soft or void areas (p. 4-58).
Cost about $7.20 per m2, about 4 percent of project cost; excavation alternative about 2.6 times the cost (p. 4-59).

sections.title: Highway Embankment on Landfill Debris
sections.summary: Manual's case history: a highway bypass embankment over two old landfills (trash 2 m and 3 m average under 0.6 m of till, SPT 10 to 14). Design with n = 0.4: WH = 225 for 6 m; 14 Mg tamper; 800 kJ/m3 gives 2.4 and 1.6 MJ/m2; 2.3 m grid gives 6 and 12 drops. Actual: 14 Mg tamper, 18 and 27 m drops, three phases, 7 drops; cost $10.25/m2.
sections.body: This is the manual's second DDC case history. A highway bypass crosses two areas of old refuse: area 1 about 61 m long under an embankment about 7 m high, and area 2 about 91 m long under 3 to 3.7 m (p. 4-59). About 0.6 m of gravelly glacial till covered the landfills; trash (metals, plastic, bags, glass, no biodegradables) averaged about 2 m thick in area 1 (1 to 3.4 m) and 3 m in area 2 (1 to 6 m), SPT 10 to 14 blows/ft, some as low as 7; water table 5.5 m deep in area 2; below lay medium-dense to dense silty sand and gravel. The landfills were 14-18 years past closure and decomposition was likely complete (p. 4-60). DDC was chosen to reduce total and differential settlement. Predicted: area 2, Eq. 4-1 with n = 0.4 for a landfill and D = 6 m gives WH = 225 Mg-m, so a 14 Mg tamper needs H = 16 m; area 1, D = 3.4 m gives H = (3.4/0.4)^2/14 = 5.2 m. Table 4-3 landfill 600-1100 kJ/m3; medium dense, so 800 kJ/m3: area 2, 3 m x 800 = 2.4 MJ/m2; area 1, 2 m x 800 = 1.6 MJ/m2. A 14 Mg tamper is typically 1.6 m in diameter, giving a 2.3 m grid; no ironing pass. Eq. 4-2: area 2, N = 5.66, 6 drops; area 1, N = 11.6, 12 drops, or 6 drops with H = 10 m (pp. 4-60 to 4-61). Expected maximum SPT 15 to 40 (Table 4-2) and induced settlement 20 percent of fill thickness (p. 4-62). Actual: site leveled and a 0.6 m silty sandy gravel working mat placed; specifications required at least a 13.6 Mg tamper with 18 m and 27 m drops; the contractor used 14 Mg, three phases (4.6 m grid, offset 2.3 m, then repeat of phase 1), 7 drops per point, giving 2.5 and 3.75 MJ/m2, more than calculated because the specified drops were higher. Craters were about 1 m in phase 1 and 0.5 m in phase 3; no heave. No post-DDC borings were made; pavements performed well with no evidence of settlement. A method specification (6 to 10 drops) was let to a specialty contractor; 7 drops sufficed; cost $10.25 per m2 ($8.57 per yd2), excluding the working mat (p. 4-63).
key_points: Eq. 4-1 with n = 0.4 (landfill) and D = 6 m gives WH = 225 Mg-m; 14 Mg tamper, H = 16 m (p. 4-60).
Table 4-3 landfill energy 800 kJ/m3 selected: 2.4 MJ/m2 (3 m) and 1.6 MJ/m2 (2 m) (p. 4-61).
Eq. 4-2 on a 2.3 m grid: N = 5.66 (6 drops) area 2; N = 11.6 (12 drops) area 1, or 6 drops with H = 10 m (p. 4-61).
Expected induced settlement 20 percent of fill thickness in landfills (p. 4-62).
Actual: 3 phases, 7 drops, 2.5 and 3.75 MJ/m2; craters 1 m then 0.5 m; no heave (p. 4-62).
Cost $10.25 per m2, excluding the 0.6 m working mat (p. 4-63).
