sections.title: Vibro-compaction
sections.summary: Part 3.0 (pp. 4-64 to 4-95) covers vibro-compaction: feasibility (applications, advantages, gradation limits), construction equipment and backfill, design by relative density and probe spacing, specifications and QA, cost, and three case histories.
sections.body: Part 3.0 of the chapter treats vibro-compaction, the in situ densification of loose granular soils with probe-type depth vibrators. It covers feasibility considerations (applications, advantages and disadvantages, geotechnical and environmental evaluations), construction equipment and backfill materials, design (relative density targets, probe spacing and patterns, performance requirements), construction specifications and quality assurance, cost information, and three case histories (pp. 4-64 to 4-95).
sections.applicability: Overview of evaluating, designing and contracting vibro-compaction.

sections.title: Feasibility Considerations
sections.summary: Vibro-compaction feasibility: transportation applications, advantages and disadvantages, and limitations of the system, with geotechnical and environmental evaluations (p. 4-64).
sections.body: Vibro-compaction can be used to achieve a number of design objectives, as discussed in the chapter introduction. This section discusses its applications for transportation facilities, its advantages and disadvantages, the limitations of the system, and its feasibility (p. 4-64).
sections.applicability: Deciding whether vibro-compaction suits a site.

sections.title: Applications
sections.summary: Thousands of U.S. vibro-compaction projects have been done, about 10 percent transportation related: foundation soils under structures, embankment fills, tunnel overburden and artificial tunnel islands, liquefaction mitigation for piles, abutments, piers and approach embankments, underwater embankment fills, and pre-settling potential cavities.
sections.body: Thousands of vibro-compaction projects have been completed in the United States, about 10 percent of them transportation related (p. 4-64). For transportation projects vibro-compaction can treat: foundation soils beneath proposed structures; highway embankment fills; tunnels, by compaction of overburden soils; densification of artificial tunnel islands; mitigation of liquefaction potential, including compaction to stabilize pile foundations driven through loose granular materials and densification for abutments, piers and approach embankment foundations; compaction of underwater embankment fills; and compaction in areas of potential cavities beneath embankments to pre-settle and fill such voids before a structure is built.
key_points: About 10 percent of U.S. vibro-compaction projects are transportation related (p. 4-64).
Uses include liquefaction mitigation for piles, abutments, piers and approach embankments.
Can compact underwater embankment fills and pre-settle potential cavities.
sections.applicability: Transportation uses of vibro-compaction.

sections.title: Advantages and Disadvantages
sections.summary: Vibro-compaction is usually cheaper and faster than deep foundations, reduces liquefaction risk, works above and below groundwater, and reaches about 165 ft (about 100 ft recommended). It works only in granular soils: densification generally fails with more than 12 to 15 percent silt or more than 2 percent clay; it needs thorough investigation with continuous SPT and/or CPT and gradations.
sections.body: Advantages (3.1.2.1): as an alternative to deep foundations it is usually more economical and often saves significant time; loads can be spread from footing level, minimizing problems from lower weak layers; densification considerably reduces seismic liquefaction risk; it is a cost-effective alternative to removing and replacing poor soils; maximum improvement of granular soils is to a depth of about 165 ft, with about 100 ft generally recommended; and it is effective above and below the groundwater level (pp. 4-64 to 4-65). Disadvantages (3.1.2.2): it is effective only in granular, cohesionless soils; realignment of the sand grains and proper densification generally cannot be achieved when the granular soil contains more than 12 to 15 percent silt OR more than 2 percent clay. The 165 ft maximum depth is rarely limiting. A thorough soil investigation is required, possibly more detailed than for deep foundations because the native soil to the full treatment depth produces the result, so the total profile must be understood; the investigation requires continuous standard penetration tests (SPT) and/or cone penetrometer tests (CPT) plus gradation tests to verify suitability (p. 4-65).
key_points: Maximum improvement depth about 165 ft; about 100 ft generally recommended (p. 4-65).
Effective above and below the natural groundwater level.
Densification generally not achieved with more than 12 to 15 percent silt OR more than 2 percent clay (p. 4-65).
Investigation needs continuous SPT and/or CPT and gradation tests (p. 4-65).
Usually more economical and faster than deep foundations (p. 4-64).
sections.applicability: Weighing vibro-compaction against deep foundations and replacement.

sections.title: Feasibility Evaluations
sections.summary: Container heading for vibro-compaction feasibility evaluations: geotechnical suitability from in situ gradation and CPT (Table 4-5, Figures 4-27, 4-28) and environmental considerations of the wet method (pp. 4-65 to 4-69).
sections.body: This heading introduces the two evaluations of vibro-compaction feasibility: geotechnical, based on the in situ soil gradation, USCS class and cone penetration test, and environmental, concerning the effluent of the wet method and soil or groundwater contaminants.
sections.applicability: Structured feasibility screening for vibro-compaction.

sections.title: Geotechnical (In Situ Soil Gradations)
sections.summary: Vibro-compaction suits granular soils with little or no fines. Table 4-5 (Degen 1997) rates USCS classes: SW ideally suited; GW well suited; GP and SP marginal if D60/D10 <= 2; GM, GC not possible if clay >2% and silt >10%; SM inhibited if silt >8%; SC inhibited if clay >2%. Figure 4-27 gradation zones A-D (zone B ideal, fines below 10 percent) and Figure 4-28 CPT chart (Massarsch 1991).
sections.body: Vibratory compaction is most effective on granular materials with little to no fines or low cohesion or plasticity. Degen (1997) proposed a quick USCS-based assessment, Table 4-5 (sources Kirsch and Kirsch 2010 and Degen 1997) (pp. 4-65 to 4-66): GW well graded gravel, well suited, with potential penetration difficulties for less powerful machines; GP poorly graded gravel, compaction only marginal if D60/D10 <= 2 (trial compaction recommended); GM, GC silty or clayey gravel, compaction not possible if clay content >2% and silt content >10%; SW well graded sand, ideally suited; SP poorly graded sand, marginal if D60/D10 <= 2 (trial compaction recommended); SM silty sand, compaction inhibited if silt content >8%; SC clayey sand, compaction inhibited if clay content >2%. Suitability has generally been judged from gradation (Figure 4-27): curves entirely within zone B are ideally suited, with fines content below 10 percent; zone A is well compactible but high gravel content and permeability may hinder penetration; zone C should be backfilled with gravel instead of sand to improve vibrator contact (the print says this drastically increases compaction time); curves partly or entirely in zone D are not readily compactable and can be improved by vibro-replacement (Chapter 5) (p. 4-67). Alternatively, CPT gives continuous tip resistance and sleeve friction; Massarsch's (1991) classification is Figure 4-28. Vibration temporarily nullifies intergranular forces so grains rearrange under gravity to a denser state, lowering void ratio and compressibility, raising friction angle, and leaving mostly elastic settlement; the reduction depends on grain shape, composition and vibration intensity (Moseley and Priebe 1993) (p. 4-68). Withdrawal forms a compact soil cylinder; the surface cone is in-filled with site soil or imported fill. Rearrangement is not possible in cohesive fine-grained soils.
key_points: Table 4-5 SW: ideally suited; GW: well suited, penetration difficulties possible with less powerful machines (p. 4-66).
Table 4-5 GP and SP: if D60/D10 <= 2 compaction only marginal; trial compaction recommended (p. 4-66).
Table 4-5 GM, GC: compaction not possible if clay content >2% and silt content >10% (p. 4-66).
Table 4-5 SM: compaction inhibited if silt content >8%; SC: inhibited if clay content >2% (p. 4-66).
Figure 4-27 zone B (entirely within): ideally suited, fines content below 10 percent (p. 4-67).
Figure 4-27 zone C: backfill with gravel; zone D: not readily compactable, use vibro-replacement (p. 4-67).
CPT suitability chart after Massarsch (1991), Figure 4-28 (p. 4-67).
Compaction by grain rearrangement is not possible in cohesive, fine-grained soils (p. 4-68).

sections.title: Environmental Considerations
sections.summary: The dry method is viable only in clean, sandy, fully saturated soils, so most work is wet; jetting effluent needs temporary containment and disposal of silt and clay; explorations should classify contaminants, and if they cannot be treated on site use another method such as dry bottom-feed stone columns.
sections.body: The dry method of vibro-compaction is only viable in clean, sandy, fully saturated soils, so the great majority of projects use the wet method (p. 4-68). Although mostly granular soils are treated, the jetting water effluent requires temporary construction provisions to contain and dispose of any silt and clay it carries. Geotechnical exploration should classify not only soil type and groundwater but also any potential contaminants in soil and groundwater. If contaminants are found, it must be decided whether they can be treated at the site during the program; if not, an alternative such as the dry bottom feed stone column technique, which produces no jetting effluent, or other solutions should be considered (p. 4-69).

Jetting effluent needs containment and disposal of silt and clay.

sections.title: Construction and Materials
sections.summary: Vibro-compaction uses crane-mounted depth vibrators and suitable backfill; this section covers the equipment and the suitability of backfill material (p. 4-69).
sections.body: The vibro-compaction process uses crane-mounted depth vibrators and appropriate backfill material. This section discusses the construction equipment and the suitability of backfill material (p. 4-69).
sections.applicability: Equipment and materials for vibro-compaction.

sections.title: Construction
sections.summary: Probe-type vibrators 12 to 16 in diameter and 10 to 15 ft long carry eccentric weights driven by motors typically 100-130 kW, generating horizontal vibration with dynamic forces of 33,750 to 100,000 lbs (150 to 450 kN) at 1,800-3,200 rpm; lower frequency, higher amplitude units densify better. Follower tubes with isolation couplings extend depth; cranes or barges carry the assembly; water or air jetting is used.
sections.body: The equipment is high-powered, probe-type vibrators 12 to 16 inches in diameter and 10 to 15 ft long (Figure 4-29, Table 4-6) (p. 4-69). Table 4-6 lists eight commercial vibrators with lengths 3.0 to 4.3 m, diameters 290 to 420 mm, weights 1000 to 2450 kg, motors 50 to 210 kW, speeds 1800 to 3600 rpm, amplitudes 5.3 to 32 mm and dynamic forces 150 to 450 kN (p. 4-70). Rotating eccentric weights on a vertical shaft, driven by a motor in the casing (Figure 4-30), produce vibration near the bottom; electric motors typically in the 100-130 kW range are used. The vibrations emanate radially in the horizontal plane; units in general use generate dynamic forces from 33,750 to 100,000 lbs (150 to 450 kN) at 1,800-3,200 rpm. For vibro-compaction, lower-frequency vibrators usually densify better because they usually have higher amplitude, and the natural frequency of most densifiable soils is closer to 1500 rpm than 3000 rpm (p. 4-71). Follower tubes of similar or lesser diameter extend the vibrator to depth, attached through an isolation coupling that stops vibration traveling up the tubes. The assembly hangs from a standard crane (Figure 4-31), a purpose-built hydraulic crawler crane, or a barge-mounted crane (Figure 4-32). Water or air jetting aids penetration and densification, so feed hoses and pumps are required (p. 4-72).
key_points: Vibrators 12 to 16 in diameter, 10 to 15 ft long (p. 4-69).
Motors typically 100-130 kW; dynamic forces 33,750 to 100,000 lbs (150 to 450 kN) at 1,800-3,200 rpm (pp. 4-70 to 4-71).
Table 4-6 range: length 3.0-4.3 m, diameter 290-420 mm, weight 1000-2450 kg, motor 50-210 kW, 1800-3600 rpm, amplitude 5.3-32 mm, dynamic force 150-450 kN (p. 4-70).
Lower frequency (higher amplitude) vibrators usually densify better; densifiable soils' natural frequency is closer to 1500 rpm (p. 4-71).

sections.title: Materials
sections.summary: Backfill fills the void made by densification; coarse material with little or no fines is best but too-large particles arch. Brown (1977) suitability number, Eq. 4-3: SN = 1.7 sqrt(3/(D50)^2 + 1/(D20)^2 + 1/(D10)^2), D in mm; Table 4-7: 0-10 excellent, 10-20 good, 20-30 fair, 30-40 poor, >50 unsuitable. Backfill normally has less than 10 percent passing #200 and no clay.
sections.body: Enough backfill must be supplied to fill the void created by densification so vibrations are transmitted into the in situ soil. Fine and coarse sands, rounded gravel, crushed stone, recycled aggregate and slag have been used; slag is cheap in places but settles slower than comparable gradations. Coarse materials with little or no fines make the best backfill, but particles that are too large arch in the annular space between follower tube and void and do not reach the tip (p. 4-72). Suitability depends on how much backfill can accumulate around the tip in a fixed time, controlled mainly by gradation through its settling rate in the wash water. Brown (1977) developed a rating from settling rate and project experience based on a suitability number, Eq. 4-3, Suitability No. = 1.7 sqrt[3/(D50)^2 + 1/(D20)^2 + 1/(D10)^2], where D50, D20 and D10 are the grain sizes in millimeters at 50, 20 and 10 percent passing (p. 4-73). Table 4-7 (Brown 1977) rates backfill: 0 to 10 excellent; 10 to 20 good; 20 to 30 fair; 30 to 40 poor; >50 unsuitable (the table prints no row for 40 to 50). Within reasonable limits, the lower the number, the faster the backfill settles and the faster the vibrator can be withdrawn while still compacting acceptably. Backfill normally consists of sand, or sand and gravel, with less than 10 percent by weight passing the #200 sieve and containing no clay.

sections.title: Design
sections.summary: Vibro-compaction design defines the problem, identifies possible solutions and sets performance requirements for the improved soil; the governing criterion may be total or differential settlement, bearing capacity, or seismic/liquefaction resistance.
sections.body: Like other ground modification methods, designing a vibro-compaction program requires defining the problem, identifying all possible solutions, and developing performance requirements for the improved soil. Depending on the project, the prime consideration may be total or differential settlement, bearing capacity, or a seismic/liquefaction resistance requirement (p. 4-73).
sections.applicability: Framing a vibro-compaction design.

sections.title: Design Considerations
sections.summary: Vibro-compaction is a potential solution for loose granular soils, especially deeper than 35 ft. Table 4-8 relates SPT N, CPT resistance, relative density, dry unit weight, friction angle, CSR causing liquefaction and shear wave velocity for very loose to very dense sand. Determine gradation (silt and clay content), existing relative density and required improvement.
sections.body: If loose granular soils are the site problem, vibro-compaction is a potential technical solution, especially if the loose deposit is deeper than 35 ft from the surface (p. 4-73). Table 4-8 relates penetration resistance to sand properties for assessing current density, feasibility and targets: very loose, loose, medium dense, dense, very dense respectively have SPT N (blows/foot, normally consolidated sand) <4, 4 to 10, 10 to 30, 30 to 50, >50; CPT cone resistance (kg/cm2 or tsf) <50, 50 to 100, 100 to 150, 150 to 200, >200; equivalent relative density (%) <15, 15 to 35, 35 to 65, 65 to 85, 85 to 100; dry unit weight (pcf) <90, 90 to 100, 100 to 115, 115 to 130, >130; friction angle (degrees) <30, printed '30 to 3235' for loose, 35 to 40, 40 to 45, >45; cyclic stress ratio causing liquefaction (Seed et al. 1983) <0.04, >0.04 to 0.12, >0.12 to 0.33, >0.33 to 0.40, none for very dense; shear wave velocity (ft/s, Debats and Sims 1997) <400, 400 to 525, 525 to 650, 650 to 740, >750 (p. 4-74). If vibro-compaction is selected, determine the gradation of the in situ soils including silt and clay content, their existing relative density or looseness, and the density improvement required and whether it is feasible.
key_points: Especially suited where the loose deposit is deeper than 35 ft (p. 4-73).

Table 4-8 relative density: <15, 15-35, 35-65, 65-85, 85-100 percent (p. 4-74).

sections.title: Design Procedure
sections.summary: Eq. 4-4 defines relative density from natural, minimum and maximum dry unit weights (ASTM D-2049). Vibro-compaction raises friction angle 5 to 10 degrees on average; Figures 4-33 and 4-34 relate relative density to tributary area and probe spacing; relative density above 85 percent is rarely needed. Targets: 60 percent slabs, tanks, embankments; 70 to 75 percent footings; 80 percent machinery and mats.
sections.body: Compressibility, shear resistance, permeability and resistance to dynamic loading of granular soil depend largely on its state of compaction, expressed as relative density, Eq. 4-4, Dr = [(gamma_d - gamma_d(min)) / (gamma_d(max) - gamma_d(min))] x [gamma_d(max) / gamma_d] x 100%, where gamma_d is the natural dry unit weight, gamma_d(min) the loosest and gamma_d(max) the densest, determined by current ASTM procedures [ASTM D-2049] (pp. 4-74 to 4-75). High relative density means high bearing resistance and low settlement; liquefaction resistance is a function of relative density; active pressure falls and passive resistance rises as it increases. Vibro-compaction increases the friction angle on average by 5 to 10 degrees and greatly reduces settlement. The tributary area each point can treat to a given relative density depends on gradation, method and vibrator, which may not be known in advance (Table 4-6). Figure 4-33 gives approximate relations between relative density, soil type and treatment area for a specific vibrator; even for heavy loading a relative density above 85 percent is unlikely to be needed (p. 4-75). Figure 4-34, based on the lower-bound silty sand gradation of Figure 4-33, estimates relative density versus probe spacing; similar charts can be made for coarser soils (p. 4-76). The designer sets requirements with an appropriate safety factor and confirmation testing; criteria to consider: 60 percent relative density for floor slabs, flat bottom tanks and embankments; 70 to 75 percent for column and bridge footings; 80 percent for machinery and mat foundations (p. 4-77).
key_points: Eq. 4-4: Dr = [(gd - gd,min)/(gd,max - gd,min)] x (gd,max/gd) x 100% (p. 4-74).
Friction angle increases on average 5 to 10 degrees with vibro-compaction (p. 4-75).

sections.title: Probe Spacing and Patterns
sections.summary: Density falls with distance from the probe, so point spacing is critical; stronger probes allow wider spacing. Equilateral triangular patterns are most efficient for large areas; square patterns need 5 to 8 percent more points. Figures 4-35 and 4-36 give typical spacing for 80 percent relative density; lower targets allow wider spacing.
sections.body: A vibro-compaction program uses various probe spacings and patterns. The distance between compaction points is critical because density generally decreases with distance from the probe; stronger vibroprobes allow wider spacing in the same soil (p. 4-77). The pattern also matters: an equilateral triangular pattern is mainly used for large areas as the most efficient, and a square pattern requires 5 to 8 percent more points for the same minimum density in large areas. Given the in situ gradation and required relative density, spacing can be determined; typical area patterns and spacings for 80 percent relative density are in Figures 4-35 and 4-36, and spacing would be wider for a lower requirement (pp. 4-77 to 4-78).

sections.title: Performance Requirements
sections.summary: Settlement, bearing and liquefaction requirements can all be expressed as a target in situ relative density; after compaction, effectiveness is verified by SPT, CPT, shear wave velocity or load tests (Chapter 5), and liquefaction potential evaluated from SPT and CSR.
sections.body: Performance requirements such as total or differential settlement, bearing resistance or reduced liquefaction potential can all be related to a desired in situ relative density (p. 4-78). After compaction, effectiveness is normally evaluated to verify contractual compliance and adequate performance under the intended loads or seismic event, using Standard Penetration Testing, cone penetrometer soundings, shear wave velocity or load tests, whose advantages and disadvantages are described in Chapter 5. Liquefaction potential can be evaluated from SPT blow counts and the cyclic stress ratio (CSR) at any depth (p. 4-79).
key_points: Settlement, bearing and liquefaction requirements map to a target relative density (p. 4-78).

sections.title: Construction Specifications and Quality Assurance
sections.summary: Container heading for vibro-compaction contracting procedures (method versus performance specifications) and quality assurance and monitoring (pp. 4-79 to 4-83).
sections.body: This heading introduces vibro-compaction contracting procedures, contrasting method-type and performance-type specifications, and the quality assurance, inspection and verification testing used during and after the work.
sections.applicability: Contracting and QA for vibro-compaction.

sections.title: Contracting Procedures
sections.summary: Under a method specification the agency details procedure and spacing and takes the risk (not advised without in-house expertise); under a performance specification the contractor chooses procedure and spacing; most are now performance based. Criteria may be relative density, SPT, CPT, column size, backfill quantity or bearing; wait at least 5 days, preferably about 10, before verification testing.
sections.body: Vibro-compaction may be done under a method-type or a performance-type specification (p. 4-79). Under a method specification the agency details a procedure and pattern spacing, invites bids from suitably equipped contractors, assumes the risk, and needs full knowledge of the technology and equipment; without that knowledge a method specification is not advised. Under a performance specification the end result is specified, the contractor assumes responsibility and chooses procedure and spacing, and in-depth agency knowledge is not needed. Variances in equipment and methods now favor placing responsibility on the contractor, and most vibro-compaction specifications today are performance based. Densification may be specified as minimum or average relative density, SPT blow count, cone resistance, size of gravel or sand column, minimum backfill added, or minimum load bearing (pp. 4-79 to 4-80); the best specification allows some variance within limits, since SPT counts can mislead in some stratifications and percentage densities are hard to measure. Verification testing immediately after densification can give misleadingly low results that increase with time (Mitchell and Solymar 1984; Debats and Sims 1997): a minimum wait of 5 days is recommended before testing, and about 10 days is preferable. A generic guide performance specification is in GeoTechTools (p. 4-80).
key_points: Method specification: agency assumes the risk; not advised without full in-house knowledge (p. 4-79).
Most vibro-compaction specifications today are performance based (p. 4-79).
Criteria: relative density, SPT, CPT, column size, backfill added, load bearing (p. 4-80).

sections.title: Quality Assurance and Monitoring
sections.summary: Inspection verifies probe depth, withdrawal and penetration rate, point locations, backfill volume and gradation, ammeter or hydraulic build-up, probe speed and vibration near structures; data loggers (Figure 4-37) record amps and time with depth. CPT is the best QA/QC method; SPT is the most used but least reliable; surface subsidence and downhole nuclear densimeters are alternatives.
sections.body: The QA plan and inspection are developed well before the work; duties depend on the specification (p. 4-80). Under a method specification the Owner's Engineer develops the QA/QC plan, reviews plans, accepts backfill and does all on-site inspection and testing; under a performance specification these fall to the Contractor, who supplies test results, and the Owner generally performs some independent verification (p. 4-81). Inspection includes verifying probe penetration depth and withdrawal rate; monitoring penetration rate as a rough indication of soil type and density; verifying point locations; monitoring backfill volume as an indication of density; verifying backfill gradation; monitoring ammeter or hydraulic pressure build-up; verifying probe speed; and verifying vibrations near existing structures are not excessive. Data logger records show uniformity with depth: time spent at each 1.5 to 2.0 ft stage depends on soil reaction (finer soils take longer), and motor current rises as soil densifies (Figure 4-37) (pp. 4-81 to 4-82). Verification methods include SPT borings, static CPT, surface subsidence, density of undisturbed samples and downhole nuclear densimeters. SPT is most widely available and used but least reliable for settlement, bearing capacity and relative density, with variable N values and scattered correlations, unrepresentative if pore pressures have not dissipated, and too coarse at the usual 5 ft intervals unless continuous sampling is specified (p. 4-83). Static CPT overcomes most of these, is relatively inexpensive, estimates settlement directly, and is the best available QA/QC method, but underestimates improvement while excess pore pressures remain. Surface subsidence shows average improvement but cannot verify footings or minimum compaction. Downhole nuclear densimeters lowered in an aluminum pipe before and after compaction give a continuous density-moisture profile within about 150 mm (6 in) of the pipe, but have limited use to date.
key_points: Nine inspection checks: penetration depth, withdrawal rate, penetration rate, point location, backfill volume, backfill gradation, ammeter or hydraulic build-up, probe speed, vibration near structures (p. 4-81).

SPT is most widely used but least reliable; usual 5 ft intervals are inadequate unless continuous (p. 4-83).
Nuclear densimeter reads density within about 150 mm (6 in) of the pipe (p. 4-83).

sections.title: Cost Information
sections.summary: Container heading for vibro-compaction cost: cost components and the estimating procedure (Table 4-9 price factors) and summary unit cost data for transportation projects (Table 4-10) (pp. 4-83 to 4-86).
sections.body: This heading introduces vibro-compaction cost information: how to build up the cost from point spacing, depth and unit price with the factors affecting price (Table 4-9), and summary unit costs for transportation projects (Table 4-10).
sections.applicability: Budgeting vibro-compaction.

sections.title: Cost Components
sections.summary: Number of points = treated area (including the perimeter zone) / effective area per point; footage = points x depth. Typical $5 per linear foot without backfill and $8 with backfill, plus mobilization, surface compaction of the upper 3 ft, extra fill and verification testing; area densification $1 to $3/yd3. Cost = (# compactions x depth x unit price) + mobilization; about 1 yd3 backfill per 5 ft; 300 ft per vibrator per 8 hour day.
sections.body: Point spacing from Section 3.3 sets the effective area per point; the total area, including the perimeter zone outside the loaded area, divided by that area gives the number of points, and points times depth gives the budget footage (p. 4-83). It is normally more economical to lower the whole site by the compaction than to add backfill from the surface. A typical price is $5 per linear foot with no backfill around the probe and $8 with granular backfill; backfill cost varies locally; add mobilization/demobilization (p. 4-84). Other costs: surface densification, since lacking overburden the upper 3 ft must be compacted by conventional surface methods; additional fill to reach grade and offset the depression; and verification testing, normally SPT (some continuous) with CPT on large projects, performed at the centroid of the points for the lowest readings, or midway between two points for an average. For typical area densification the cost is $1 to $3/yd3 of densified soil, depending on project size, gradation and degree of densification, higher in marginal soils needing special backfill. Table 4-9 lists price factors: in situ material (type, density, cementation); backfill (type, cost); densification requirements (load bearing; average and minimum relative density); project requirements (size, depth, overburden, footing or area compaction, specifications, location: labor, equipment availability, freezing weather); and pricing (spacing; unit price per linear foot or cubic yard) (p. 4-85). Estimating procedure: determine the performance requirement; the number of points from it, the spacing and project size; the depth; then cost = (# of compactions x depth x unit price) + mobilization. The price includes supervision, labor, equipment, tools, utilities and backfill added during compaction, about 1 cubic yard per 5 linear feet; production is about 300 linear feet per vibrator per 8 hour day; add fill to raise grade (p. 4-86).

sections.title: Case Histories
sections.summary: The manual presents three vibro-compaction case histories representing different transportation applications: fill beneath a covered-roadway footing, a port container yard on replaced marsh deposits, and an airport terminal on liquefiable sands.
sections.body: The vibro-compaction technique is used to achieve a variety of design objectives, and the case histories selected for the chapter represent different transportation applications: densifying embankment fill under a large pier footing for a covered roadway, densifying hydraulically placed sand backfill in a dredged-out marsh for a container storage yard, and mitigating liquefaction under an airport terminal (p. 4-86).
sections.applicability: Worked vibro-compaction applications in transportation projects.

sections.title: Case History: Vibro-Compacted Fill Beneath a Covered-Roadway Pier Footing
sections.summary: Manual's case history (Hayward Baker 1989): a 300 ft by 30 ft footing designed for 5,960 psf on about 20 ft of loose to medium dense silty gravelly sand fill was supported by vibro-compaction with stone backfill: 540 points, 120 kW vibrator, 15 to 20 ft deep, 6 ft grid; plate load tests gave about 0.5 in settlement against a 3/4 in limit.
sections.body: This is the manual's first vibro-compaction case history (Hayward Baker 1989). An interstate improvement used deep-cut, covered roadways supporting landscaped parks; massive on-grade pier footings carried the roadway section and the lateral load of embankment soils behind the wall (pp. 4-86 to 4-87). For two units of a 2,590 ft roadway section, a 300 ft long by 30 ft wide footing was to bear on existing highway embankment fill at an assumed allowable 5,960 psf, but investigation found the loose to medium-dense silty, gravelly, fine-to-medium sand fill (about 20 ft deep) could not carry it without extensive settlement. Deep foundations and in situ improvement were considered, and vibro-compaction was chosen on time and cost. Stone backfill was specified; at 540 compaction points a 120 kW vibrator densified soils to an average of 15 to 20 ft (Figure 4-38) (p. 4-87), through the fill and the loose top of the underlying sandy glacial deposit. Treatment extended 10 to 20 ft beyond the footing, with points on a 6 ft grid to limit settlement to 3/4 inch. Two plate load tests with a 6 ft by 6 ft plate over compaction points, loaded to 210,000 lbf (5,960 psf), gave average total settlement about 0.5 inch under working load and about 1/4 inch permanent deformation on unloading (p. 4-88).
key_points: Design bearing 5,960 psf on about 20 ft of loose to medium-dense silty gravelly sand fill (p. 4-87).
540 points, 120 kW vibrator, stone backfill, depth 15 to 20 ft, 6 ft grid (pp. 4-87 to 4-88).
Treatment extended 10 to 20 ft beyond the footing; settlement limit 3/4 in (p. 4-88).
Plate load tests (6 ft x 6 ft to 210,000 lbf): about 0.5 in total, about 1/4 in permanent (p. 4-88).

sections.title: Case History: Port Container Yard on Dredged-and-Replaced Marsh Deposits
sections.summary: Manual's case history (Hussin and Foshee 1994): a 109,300 m2 container yard over virgin marsh was built by dredging soft clay to -25 ft, backfilling underwater with clean sand (less than 1 percent clay, less than 5 percent fines), wick drains on 5 ft centers to -40 ft, and vibro-compaction lowering the surface from 35 to 31 ft; CPTs confirmed the densification.
sections.body: This is the manual's second vibro-compaction case history (Hussin and Foshee 1994). A port terminal expansion included a 267,000 yd2 (225,000 m2) concrete-paved container yard in three areas; two former marshlands, filled and surcharged over 10 years earlier, needed no more improvement, but Area C, about 131,000 yd2 (109,300 m2), was virgin marsh (pp. 4-88 to 4-89). Filled marshland in the region had subsided 2 to 4 inches (50-100 mm) per year, which the owner would not accept, so replacing marsh mud with less compressible soil was the only option. The profile (Figures 4-40, 4-41) had extremely soft, compressible marsh mud over a firmer clay and a highly overconsolidated, virtually incompressible marl (p. 4-90). The program had three steps: dredge the soft clay to -25 ft (-7.5 m) and replace it with 1.2 million cubic yards of clean sand to +10 ft (+3 m); install wick drains; and densify the very loose sand by vibro-compaction, avoiding dewatering (Figure 4-42) (p. 4-91). Wick drains to -40 ft (-12.2 m) MLW on 5 ft (1.5 m) centers gave estimated post-construction settlement of 3.5 to 7 inches primary over 2 years and up to 4 inches secondary over 50 years. The underwater fill was specified as fine sand with less than 1 percent clay and less than 5 percent fines (silt and clay), placed hydraulically (p. 4-92). Four rigs working double shifts, 6 days a week for 5 months, densified it, lowering the surface from 35 to 31 ft (10.7 to 9.5 m). Pre- and post-treatment CPTs confirmed the required densification (Figure 4-43), which also guarded against earthquake liquefaction. Backfilling through water and vibro-compacting proved as effective as and much cheaper than dewatering and placing compacted layers (p. 4-93).

sections.title: Case History: Airport Terminal on Liquefiable Sands
sections.summary: Manual's case history (Sobel et al. 1993): a 160,000 ft2 terminal on clean, uniform, saturated fine-to-medium sands (12 to 45 ft) with FS against liquefaction below 1 and 1 ft potential settlement. Criteria M 6.0, 0.12g, FS 2.0, 1 in total and 0.5 in differential settlement; 10 ft by 10 ft grid to 26 and 36 ft, over 2,600 points; SPT rose with time.
sections.body: This is the manual's third vibro-compaction case history (Sobel et al. 1993). A new 160,000 ft2 (15,000 m2) airport terminal over loose, sandy, potentially liquefiable soils needed ground improvement (p. 4-94). Borings found delta-deposited, clean, uniformly graded, saturated fine-to-medium sands from 12 to 45 ft (3.7 to 13.7 m). Using Seed et al. (1985) for the factor of safety and Tokimatsu and Seed (1987) for volumetric strain, the factor of safety against liquefaction was below unity and volumetric strain of 10 percent of the layer gave about 1 ft (0.3 m) of potential settlement. Deep foundations were rejected for cost and uncertain performance under liquefaction; of the improvement alternatives (excavation/replacement, dynamic compaction, deep blasting, compaction grouting) vibro-compaction was chosen for cost-effectiveness and its record in sands. Criteria: design earthquake magnitude 6.0, peak ground acceleration 0.12g, minimum factor of safety against liquefaction 2.0, allowable differential settlement 0.5 inch (12 mm) and total 1 inch (25 mm). Points were on a 10 ft by 10 ft (3 m by 3 m) grid to depths of 26 ft (8 m) and 36 ft (11 m), selected from performance studies of sites where liquefaction had occurred rather than to the full 45 ft. Spacing was reduced where post-treatment tests showed loose conditions remaining (p. 4-95). Over 2,600 points were made; 34 post-treatment SPTs at about 1100 yd2 (900 m2) intervals at grid centroids generally showed compliance. Low values at 12 to 17 ft were attributed to a dense coarse sand crust temporarily arching over loose material, and after waiting 1 to 3 weeks most N values had increased to meet the criteria.
